sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities were mixed in a volatile, policy-driven week as the Fed's first rate hike in three years and 10-year UST yields briefly above **5%** offset a firm finish. MSCI World ended roughly flat, with MSCI Developed Markets similar and MSCI Emerging Markets modestly firmer. The S&P 500 slipped about **0.1%** to **7,650.50** and the Dow lost **1.7%** in its worst week since March, while the Nasdaq rose **0.7%** and the MAG7 cohort was mixed but led Friday's rebound. Euro Stoxx 50 closed near **6,325**, China's CSI 300 around **4,507**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged higher and Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed to **65,102**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities finished a choppy week mixed. The S&P 500 slipped about **0.1%** to **7,650.50** and the Dow shed **1.7%** to **51,682.64**, its third straight weekly loss and worst since March, while the Nasdaq bucked the trend with a **0.7%** gain as investors rotated back toward mega-cap technology.

The dominant driver was Wednesday's FOMC, where the Fed raised rates by **25bps** for the first time in three years and paired it with a hawkish dot plot: 16 of 18 officials projected at least one further hike this year and a median end-2026 funds rate of **4.125%**, alongside upgraded inflation forecasts. Bond markets read the message as more hawkish than expected, with the policy-sensitive 2-year yield up roughly **10bps** and the 10-year briefly above **5%**, its highest since July 2007.

Leadership favoured growth over value on Friday's bounce, with technology and communication services outperforming while rate-sensitive and smaller-cap names lagged, the Russell 2000 easing **0.53%** on the day. Elevated crude and yields kept sentiment cautious through midweek despite still-resilient earnings.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities held up better than the macro noise implied, supported by a resilient growth backdrop. Eurozone Q2 GDP was confirmed at **0.6%** sequentially, with Ireland, Slovenia and Lithuania leading, while UK output rose **0.4%** in July, beating expectations for no growth and accelerating from June's **0.3%**.

The Euro Stoxx 50 closed around **6,325**, firming into Friday even as global yields climbed. ECB commentary underscored a data-dependent stance, with policymaker Vujcic noting that market bets on further hikes largely reflect higher energy prices rather than broad-based pressure.

Regional dispersion persisted: elevated energy costs and high gilt yields remained headwinds for the UK ahead of the Autumn Budget, keeping borrowing costs and fiscal concerns in focus even as domestic activity surprised to the upside.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japan set the tone as the BoJ raised its policy rate by **25bps** to **1.25%** on Friday, its highest in 31 years, but framed the move dovishly with two dissenters and little urgency for further tightening. The Nikkei 225 rose **1.51%** on the day to **65,102**, extending gains into the decision as the well-flagged hike removed uncertainty.

China and Hong Kong advanced, with the CSI 300 up **1.06%** to **4,507.39** and the Hang Seng edging higher, while MSCI's Asia Pacific benchmark added about **0.8%**, aided by the strongest US tech performance since early August.

Policy signals dominated the regional narrative, with the yen initially strengthening toward **JPY 153** early in the week before the dovish BoJ outcome sent USD/JPY back up, underscoring sensitivity to rate-differential expectations and the tech cycle.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar firmed after the hawkish Fed hike. The unanimous **25bp** move, a dot plot showing 16 of 18 officials expecting more and a median **4.125%** end-2026 rate lifted US yields and reinforced the greenback, reversing an earlier-week dip that had briefly carried EUR/USD to a seven-week high on softer oil.

The yen was the standout mover: after appreciating toward **JPY 153** early in the week, USD/JPY jumped over **2%** as the BoJ's dovish hike and lack of urgency around further tightening left the currency exposed.

Sterling delivered a mixed performance, driven more by global macro dynamics than UK-specific news, firming against oil-sensitive crosses as crude fell but ceding ground to the resurgent dollar.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy was the dominant theme as crude reversed the prior week's spike. Brent fell **4.3%** to **$99.71** and WTI dropped **2.9%** to **$95.24** after China, acting on a Saudi request, urged Iran to limit Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, easing the geopolitical premium and cooling inflation fears.

Gold advanced **0.7%** to **$4,377.25**, spiking as high as around **$4,380**, its first weekly gain in four weeks as falling oil, a softer post-Fed dollar and lower yields boosted its appeal despite the hawkish policy backdrop.

Industrial metals rebounded, with copper volatile as traders awaited a US decision on refined-copper tariffs after LME prices had earlier hit a record near **$14,617** per tonne on tariff speculation.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign yields dominated the week. The 10-year UST climbed above **5%** to its highest since July 2007 earlier in the period, and the rate-sensitive 2-year rose about **10bps** after the FOMC as markets judged the decision more hawkish than expected, flattening pressure building across the curve.

Yields later pared as oil eased, with the 10-year slipping roughly **9bps** to about **4.93%** on Thursday, helped by a Bank of England hold that supported gilts. Markets priced around a **90%** chance of a further Fed hike by the December meeting and a **55%** chance as soon as October.

The rate volatility kept credit cautious, with the higher-yield backdrop and firmer Treasuries leaving IG relatively resilient while HY sentiment stayed sensitive to the hawkish policy path.
